title: Saccaka's boast
hook: a famous debater boasts he will shake the Buddha, and sweats instead

segments.voice: Yesterday: gopalaka, and your line, know your herd. Eleven plain skills of a cowherd, each a skill of mind.

In the city of Vesali lives a debater named Saccaka, and he is very good. He says so himself. There's no teacher alive, he tells crowds, who wouldn't shake and tremble if he debated them. Even a post, he says, would shake if he argued with it, never mind a human being. Then he hears what the Buddha teaches, and announces he'll drag him around like a man dragging a sheep by its fleece. Five hundred people come to watch.
screen: `A DEBATER IN VESALI.` → `EVEN A POST WOULD SHAKE.` → `FIVE HUNDRED COME TO WATCH.`

segments.voice: This is the shorter discourse to Saccaka, the thirty-fifth of the Middle-Length Sayings. Saccaka opens: the body is my self, and so are feeling, perception, mental formations and consciousness. The Buddha doesn't argue back at once. He asks a question. A king rules his country; can he have someone executed, fined or banished? Of course, says Saccaka. Then you say the body is your self. Can you command it: let my body be like this, don't let it be like that? Saccaka goes silent. The Buddha asks again. Silence again. The text adds a dramatic touch: a spirit named Vajirapani hovers above with a thunderbolt, and only Saccaka and the Buddha can see him. The Buddha asks a third time, and Saccaka answers: no. I can't command it. Then the same for feeling, perception, formations, consciousness. If it can't be commanded, and it changes, and it brings pain when it changes, is it fit to call it mine, I, my self? No. At the end, sweat pours from Saccaka's forehead, soaks through his robe and drips to the ground. The Buddha notes, gently, that there's no sweat on his own body. And someone in the crowd says Saccaka looks like a crab with its legs broken, unable to crawl back into its pond. But Saccaka isn't a villain. He invites the Buddha and the monks to a meal the next day, and later comes back for another talk, which we hear tomorrow. Certainty that has never been tested can sweat when it finally is.
screen: `THE BODY IS MY SELF, SAYS SACCAKA` · `A KING RULES; CAN YOU RULE YOUR BODY?` · `SILENCE, THEN NO` · `SWEAT ON HIS ROBE, NONE ON THE BUDDHA` · then, large: `THE SWEAT OF CERTAINTY.`

segments.voice: Try the Buddha's question on yourself: tell your body, don't let this knee ache, don't let my mind wander, and watch the next minute. Notice the body and mind doing what they do, commanded or not, and if a little thought of I'm good at this shows up, let it pass too, like Saccaka's crowd going home.
Saccaka's boast. The debater who said even a post would shake before him, and ended up sweating, then coming back for more.
Your line: the sweat of certainty. Even Saccaka came back for more. That's day four hundred thirty.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use MN 35's question, whether we can command the body and mind to be as we wish, as a classic way into the teaching of not-self (anatta) and the five aggregates.

fork.setup: you're Saccaka. the Buddha asks: can you command your body, 'let it be like this, not like that'? five hundred people are watching. what do you do?
options: change the subject to the weather.
fork.reveal: Saccaka stays silent twice. asked a third time, he admits: no. then the sweat starts.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about the Buddha winning a debate.
what it means: what changes, can't be commanded and brings pain isn't fit to be called 'mine, I, my self'.

what a scholar hears: Saccaka is called a son of the Niganthas (the Jain tradition) and an Aggivessana by clan, and his question-and-answer here closely echoes the discourse on the characteristic of not-self (SN 22.59), which tradition counts as the Buddha's second sermon.

chat.says: Why did the Buddha say the body isn't really your self?
options: You can't command it to be this way or that, and it changes and brings pain.
Because the spirit with the thunderbolt warned him not to call it his.
Because Saccaka lost the debate, so the Buddha's view won by default.
chat.meaning: In MN 35 Saccaka admits he can't command his body. What can't be commanded, changes, and brings pain isn't fit to call mine, I, my self.

Vesali.meaning: the city where Saccaka lived and debated

Vajirapani.meaning: a spirit with a thunderbolt, seen only by Saccaka and the Buddha

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 35, Culasaccaka Sutta (the shorter discourse to Saccaka)
Samyutta Nikaya 22.59, Anattalakkhana Sutta (the characteristic of not-self)

notes: MN 35 paraphrased: Saccaka's boast (even an insentient post would shake), the 'sheep by the fleece' image, the king simile, Vajirapani with the thunderbolt, the sweat, Dummukha's crab simile, the meal invitation. Confirm each detail. The crowd size (five hundred Licchavis) also to confirm.
Vajirapani is described as a spirit (yakkha); the script says 'a spirit' to keep it plain.
Saccaka's family background (son of Nigantha parents) is stated neutrally; Jain sources do not record this debate.
